value.overview: The Yellow-bellied Flycatcher (Empidonax flaviventris) is a small North American tyrant flycatcher that breeds in cool, wet boreal forests and winters in Mexico and Central America. It is compact and olive-green, with a conspicuous pale eye-ring, whitish wingbars, and yellowish underparts. Like other Empidonax flycatchers, it is often identified most reliably by its voice, habitat, and range. In Costa Rica it occurs as a nonbreeding migrant rather than a breeding resident.
value.classification: The Yellow-bellied Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Empidonax. It is one of several closely similar small insect-eating flycatchers in this genus.
value.identification: This small, compact flycatcher is about 13–15 cm long, with a relatively large head, short tail, and broad-based bill. The upperparts are yellowish olive, while the underparts are yellow-washed from the throat through the belly, although worn individuals may appear duller. A strong whitish eye-ring and two pale wingbars are important field marks. It often sits quietly in dense vegetation, makes quick head movements, and sallies out to catch insects. Voice is especially useful for separating it from similar Empidonax species.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds across much of Canada and the northeastern and north-central United States, especially in wet coniferous forest, spruce-fir swamps, bogs, peatlands, and openings with mossy ground. During the nonbreeding season it moves through Mexico into Central America, using humid lowland and montane evergreen forest, dense second growth, forest edges, and shaded coffee plantations. In Costa Rica, it is a regular seasonal migrant and winter visitor, occurring in suitable forested habitats across the country, including foothill and middle-elevation sites; it does not normally breed there.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds reach Costa Rica mainly during the northern winter, generally from about September or October through April or May, and return north to breed in spring. Costa Rica is part of the species’ nonbreeding range, not its breeding range.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in wet northern forests, particularly spruce or fir stands associated with bogs, swamps, peatlands, and mossy ground. The female builds a small open cup, commonly placed low in vegetation or on a moss-covered stump, bank, or other support near the ground. The nest is made from moss, plant fibers, grasses, and other fine materials and is often well concealed. Both adults feed the nestlings, which are primarily supplied with insects.
value.dietFeeding: The Yellow-bellied Flycatcher feeds mainly on flying and foliage-dwelling insects, including flies, mosquitoes, moths, beetles, ants, and other small arthropods. It usually forages from low or middle levels of dense vegetation. From a quiet perch, it makes short flights to seize prey in the air or from leaves, sometimes hovering briefly. During migration and winter it may also consume small berries or other fruit when available.
value.behavior: This species is generally inconspicuous and spends much of its time perched quietly in dense forest understory. It frequently turns its head, flicks its tail, and makes short, purposeful sallies after insects, often returning to the same perch. It is more readily detected by its sharp call than by movement or song. Territorial singing is associated mainly with the breeding season; in Costa Rica, migrants are usually quiet or give brief call notes rather than sustained breeding song.

conservation.populationTrend: Available continent-wide monitoring and modeling indicate an overall stable to increasing population pattern, although trends can vary among regions and wintering areas.
